Default Loss Guarantee: shared risk, capped and clocked

After this lesson you can:
  • Explain what a DLG is and why RBI regulates it tightly
  • State the eligibility, form, cap and invocation rules
  • Identify the duties the RE can never delegate to a DLG

Learning rhythm: read one section at a time, pause to explain the control in your own words, then answer the knowledge check without looking back.

On this page
  1. The economics and the danger
  2. The rulebook
  3. In the platform
  4. Regulatory anchors

1. The economics and the danger

In many RE–LSP partnerships the LSP believes in 'its' borrowers and offers to absorb first losses: a Default Loss Guarantee.

Useful — it aligns incentives and lets REs enter segments they'd otherwise avoid.

Dangerous — unbounded DLG turns the RE into a rent-a-licence: the LSP effectively lends, unregulated, behind the RE's badge.

That is precisely what the RBI's DLG framework prevents.

2. The rulebook

The framework's teeth:

  • Eligible providers and contracts — a proper agreement with an LSP meeting eligibility norms.
  • Permitted forms only — cash deposit with the RE, fixed deposit with lien, or bank guarantee. Promises and comfort letters are not DLG.
  • The 5% cap — DLG cannot exceed 5% of the outstanding portfolio it covers. First-loss beyond that is structurally prohibited.
  • The 120-day clock — the RE must invoke the guarantee within 120 days of a default, or the cover lapses for that case.
  • Disclosure — DLG arrangements are disclosed; portfolio performance stays transparent.

And the non-delegable core: NPA classification and provisioning stay with the RE. A loss covered by DLG is still an NPA on the RE's book — the guarantee compensates; it never launders asset quality.

3. In the platform

LoanOS models DLG as a governed object: provider eligibility, form, cap tracking against the covered portfolio, invocation windows with clocks, replenishment, recovery-sharing and disclosure evidence — implemented in the core DLG module with the exposure math and clocks the framework demands. A BA scoping a DLG-backed program specifies the covered portfolio definition precisely: caps and invocations compute against it.

Regulatory anchors

  • RBI-LSP-DLG — DLG eligibility, permitted forms, 5% portfolio cap, 120-day invocation, disclosure, RE-retained classification duty.

Family IDs resolve in the India regulatory register (docs/compliance/india-regulatory-register.md), which owns sources and caveats.

Where this lives in LoanOS

Retrieval practice

Knowledge check

Answer aloud or write your choice before opening the explanation. If you miss it, revisit the named section—not the whole lesson.

1. An LSP offers to guarantee 12% of first losses on its sourced portfolio. What does the platform do?

  1. Accept — more cover is safer
  2. Accept with disclosure
  3. Reject — DLG is capped at 5% of the portfolio
  4. Convert to co-lending
Reveal answer and reasoning

C. The 5% cap is structural: beyond it, the arrangement becomes de facto unlicensed lending by the LSP, which the framework exists to prevent.

2. A DLG fully covers a defaulted loan. Its classification on the RE's book?

  1. Standard — no loss
  2. NPA per IRACP, regardless of the guarantee
  3. Off-book
  4. The LSP's problem
Reveal answer and reasoning

B. Classification duty is retained by the RE; DLG compensates losses but never changes asset quality.
